bibl.title: Mapping global trends in vaccine confidence and investigating barriers to vaccine uptake: a large-scale retrospective temporal modelling study

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: VACCINE CONFIDENCE as a globally comparable quantity - 290 surveys, 149 countries, 284,381 individuals, pooled into one time series
span.quote: In this large-scale retrospective data-driven analysis, we examined global trends in vaccine confidence using data from 290 surveys done between September, 2015, and December, 2019, across 149 countries, and including 284 381 individuals.

span.label: whether public confidence in the importance, safety and effectiveness of vaccines can be tracked across countries and over time, and which component predicts uptake
span.quote: Although immunisation coverage is reported administratively across the world, no similarly robust monitoring system exists for vaccine confidence.

span.label: estimates of vaccine confidence for 149 countries between 2015 and 2019, and the finding that confidence in IMPORTANCE - not safety or effectiveness - carries the strongest association with uptake
span.quote: Confidence in the importance of vaccines (rather than in their safety or effectiveness) had the strongest univariate association with vaccine uptake compared with other determinants considered.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Between November, 2015, and December, 2019, we estimate that confidence in the importance, safety, and effectiveness of vaccines fell in Afghanistan, Indonesia, Pakistan, the Philippines, and South Korea. We found significant increases in respondents strongly disagreeing that vaccines are safe between 2015 and 2019 in six countries: Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, and Serbia.

span.label: confidence in vaccines rising and falling by country on a timescale of years, and doing so unevenly across its three components
span.quote: Between November, 2015, and December, 2019, we estimate that confidence in the importance, safety, and effectiveness of vaccines fell in Afghanistan, Indonesia, Pakistan, the Philippines, and South Korea. We found significant increases in respondents strongly disagreeing that vaccines are safe between 2015 and 2019 in six countries: Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, and Serbia.

span.label: 290 surveys harmonised onto their extreme response categories, modelled with a Bayesian multinomial logit Gaussian process, with univariate Bayesian logistic regressions linking confidence and other putative drivers to uptake
span.term: 290 surveys harmonised onto their extreme response categories, modelled with a Bayesian multinomial logit Gaussian process, with univariate Bayesian logistic regressions linking confidence and other putative drivers to uptake
span.quote: In this large-scale retrospective data-driven analysis, we examined global trends in vaccine confidence using data from 290 surveys done between September, 2015, and December, 2019, across 149 countries, and including 284 381 individuals.

span.label: the study exists because THE THING IT MEASURES HAS NO ADMINISTRATIVE RECORD: `although immunisation coverage is reported administratively across the world, NO SIMILARLY ROBUST MONITORING SYSTEM EXISTS FOR VACCINE CONFIDENCE`. Coverage is counted; confidence has to be surveyed
span.quote: Although immunisation coverage is reported administratively across the world, no similarly robust monitoring system exists for vaccine confidence.

span.label: and the component that predicts uptake is not the one the public debate is about: `confidence in the IMPORTANCE of vaccines (RATHER THAN in their SAFETY or EFFECTIVENESS) had the strongest univariate association with vaccine uptake`
span.quote: Confidence in the importance of vaccines (rather than in their safety or effectiveness) had the strongest univariate association with vaccine uptake compared with other determinants considered.

span.label: THE COMPARABILITY OF 290 DIFFERENTLY-WORDED SURVEYS RESTS ON AN ASSUMPTION THE AUTHORS SAY IS UNTESTED: `we have made A KEY ASSUMPTION that, presented with different options between the extreme categories ... respondents with the strongest sentiment will fall into one of these extreme groups REGARDLESS OF ADDITIONAL CATEGORIES ... ALTHOUGH IT NEEDS TESTING FOR VALIDATION - it POOLS vaccination beliefs among those without the strongest beliefs, MASKING POTENTIALLY KEY INFORMATION`
span.quote: First, as not all surveys used have consistent responses, we have made a key assumption that, presented with different options between the extreme categories of “strongly agree” and “strongly disagree” (which are consistent across all surveys), respondents with the strongest sentiment will fall into one of these extreme groups regardless of additional categories. While this approach probably allows meaningful comparison across surveys—although it needs testing for validation—it pools vaccination beliefs among those without the strongest beliefs, masking potentially key information.

span.label: the outcome is COARSER THAN THE QUESTION: uptake means only `whether A PARENT HAS HAD ANY OF THEIR CHILDREN vaccinated against AT LEAST ONE childhood disease`, so no vaccine-specific or child-specific determinant can be investigated - and it relies on PARENTAL RECALL being accurate and its errors constant across countries
span.quote: Second, the WGM survey data only permit an investigation of uptake defined as whether a parent has had any of their children vaccinated against at least one childhood disease. These uptake data are therefore not defined on a vaccine or child-by-child basis, precluding an investigation of determinants of vaccine-specific or child-specific uptake (which has been done recently in the literature 22 , 24 , 41 ). Moreover, we rely on parental recall being accurate, and patterns of recall error not varying substantially across countries.

span.label: and religion, one of the four named drivers, was `RECODED INTO THE LARGEST AND MINORITY GROUPS` because of low case counts - so the religious finding is about majority-versus-minority status, not about any religion
span.quote: Finally, owing to low case counts of respondents who have not had their children vaccinated ( appendix 2 ) and the varying religious groups across countries, religious groups were recoded into the largest and minority groups to extract results from our regression analysis.

span.label: THE TERM THE PROJECT'S OWN DEFINITION PAPER REJECTED IS NOW THE HEADLINE CONSTRUCT, AND THE TWO ARE JOINED BY `OR`: five instruments are described as `used to measure CONFIDENCE OR HESITANCY`. macdonald2015 - same research group - refused `confidence` as the name because it covers `ONLY ONE CATEGORY of factors`, and larson2015 has a numbered rule that refusal is not hesitancy
span.quote: The VCI survey is one of a diverse set of metrics and indices used to measure confidence or hesitancy such as the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines Survey, which measures vaccine hesitancy among parents; 19 the Vaccination Confidence Scale, which measures confidence in adolescent vaccination; 20 the 5-C scale (confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility), which identifies psychological barriers of vaccination behaviour; 21 and the SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale, which has been deployed across multiple countries.

span.label: the Likert options genuinely differed between surveys and only the two extreme categories were consistent across all of them
span.quote: Likert responses presented to respondents differed between surveys ( appendix 1 p 4 ); however, the outermost categories (“strongly agree” and “strongly disagree”) remained consistent across surveys.

span.label: the harmonisation rests on an assumption the paper states but does not test - that respondents at the extremes would not have answered differently under a finer scale
span.quote: This reclassification assumes that respondents who report the most confident (“strongly agree”) and least confident (“strongly disagree”) beliefs are unlikely to change their response regardless of whether they are presented with additional Likert categories such as “tend to agree”, “somewhat agree”, or “neither agree nor disagree” (or a combination thereof; appendix 1 p 4 ).

span.label: only three confidence statements could be used because the religious-compatibility item was not asked in the survey supplying half the data
span.quote: As data on perceptions about the religious compatibility of vaccines was not posed to respondents in the Wellcome Global Monitor, we only consider three statements on vaccine confidence. † For this question, vaccine-preventable diseases were given as examples to respondents, which varied by country (see appendix 1 pp 28–29 ).

span.label: three survey modes were mixed - online, telephone and face to face - across the same pooled estimate
span.quote: Online, telephone, and face-to-face survey methodologies were used (see appendix 1 pp 3–4 for further details on survey methodologies).

span.label: country coverage is deeply uneven in time: one country has six timepoints while 67 have only one
span.quote: One country was surveyed over six different timepoints (Philippines), 13 countries were surveyed over four timepoints, 28 over three timepoints, 40 over two timepoints, and 67 once.

span.label: harmonising 290 surveys with different response options onto their shared extreme categories
span.note: eliminates: nothing that has been demonstrated - the authors call it `A KEY ASSUMPTION`, say it `NEEDS TESTING FOR VALIDATION`, and name its cost: it POOLS the middle and MASKS POTENTIALLY KEY INFORMATION · outcome: failed
span.quote: First, as not all surveys used have consistent responses, we have made a key assumption that, presented with different options between the extreme categories of “strongly agree” and “strongly disagree” (which are consistent across all surveys), respondents with the strongest sentiment will fall into one of these extreme groups regardless of additional categories. While this approach probably allows meaningful comparison across surveys—although it needs testing for validation—it pools vaccination beliefs among those without the strongest beliefs, masking potentially key information.

span.label: whether the association with uptake belongs to confidence as a whole or to one of its components
span.note: eliminates: the undifferentiated reading - IMPORTANCE carries the association, `rather than` safety or effectiveness, which are the components the public debate is about · outcome: held
span.quote: Confidence in the importance of vaccines (rather than in their safety or effectiveness) had the strongest univariate association with vaccine uptake compared with other determinants considered.

span.label: whether religion-specific effects could be estimated
span.note: eliminates: nothing - low case counts forced recoding `into the LARGEST AND MINORITY GROUPS`, so the finding is about majority status and not about any religion · outcome: failed
span.quote: Finally, owing to low case counts of respondents who have not had their children vaccinated ( appendix 2 ) and the varying religious groups across countries, religious groups were recoded into the largest and minority groups to extract results from our regression analysis.

span.label: recoding every intermediate Likert response into a single middle category so only `strongly agree` and `strongly disagree` are compared across surveys
span.note: eliminates: apparent trend differences that are really differences in how many response options a given survey offered · outcome: held
span.quote: Thus, to allow meaningful comparisons in trends between surveys, individual survey responses falling between “strongly agree” and “strongly disagree” were recoded into the new category “neither strongly agree nor strongly disagree”, with the “strongly agree” and “strongly disagree” responses remaining unchanged.

span.label: recoding `do not know` answers about a child's vaccination to `no`
span.note: eliminates: inflation of reported uptake by counting uncertainty as vaccination · outcome: held
span.quote: If respondent has children: “…have any of your children ever received a vaccine that was supposed to prevent them from getting childhood diseases…?

span.label: recoding religion WITHIN each country into largest, minority and refused rather than by denomination
span.note: eliminates: treating the same denomination as majority in one country and minority in another - the variable becomes social position rather than creed · outcome: held
span.quote: For each country, religion is recoded into the most frequently reported religion in a given country (largest), all other religious affiliations (minority), or refusal to answer (refused) Other Education Years in education grouped into <9 years, 9–15 years, and ≥16 years <9 years Science education: “Have you…learned about science at [school]?

span.label: vaccine confidence
span.quote: Although immunisation coverage is reported administratively across the world, no similarly robust monitoring system exists for vaccine confidence.

span.label: Vaccine Confidence Index
span.quote: These findings have resulted in the development of a Vaccine Confidence Index (VCI) survey tool (first implemented in 2015 14 ) to measure individual perceptions on the safety, importance, effectiveness, and religious compatibility of vaccines. The VCI questionnaire has the primary focus of measuring confidence across multiple countries while being minimal, thus allowing ready integration into existing global surveys.

span.label: SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale
span.quote: The VCI survey is one of a diverse set of metrics and indices used to measure confidence or hesitancy such as the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines Survey, which measures vaccine hesitancy among parents; 19 the Vaccination Confidence Scale, which measures confidence in adolescent vaccination; 20 the 5-C scale (confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility), which identifies psychological barriers of vaccination behaviour; 21 and the SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale, which has been deployed across multiple countries.

span.label: Wellcome Global Monitor
span.quote: Of the 290 surveys, 144 were collected as part of the 2018 Wellcome Global Monitor (WGM; appendix 2) . 28 In addition to probing individuals' perceptions on vaccine confidence across the globe, the WGM also surveys individuals on a range of factors including sources of trust, information-seeking behaviours, and whether respondents with children report having vaccinated at least one child against any routine immunisation programme (if the respondent reports having at least one child).

span.label: vaccine confidence - HERE, TRUST IN THE IMPORTANCE, SAFETY AND EFFECTIVENESS OF VACCINES, plus religious compatibility. Four components, and the VCI is built to measure exactly those four `while being MINIMAL, thus allowing ready integration into existing global surveys`. THE INSTRUMENT'S SHORTNESS IS A DESIGN GOAL, not a compromise
span.quote: These findings have resulted in the development of a Vaccine Confidence Index (VCI) survey tool (first implemented in 2015 14 ) to measure individual perceptions on the safety, importance, effectiveness, and religious compatibility of vaccines. The VCI questionnaire has the primary focus of measuring confidence across multiple countries while being minimal, thus allowing ready integration into existing global surveys.

span.label: FIVE INSTRUMENTS FOR TWO CONSTRUCTS, IN ONE SENTENCE, JOINED BY `OR`: the VCI, the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines Survey, the Vaccination Confidence Scale, the 5-C scale, and THE SAGE VACCINE HESITANCY SCALE - which this corpus holds as larson2015. `used to measure CONFIDENCE OR HESITANCY`
span.quote: The VCI survey is one of a diverse set of metrics and indices used to measure confidence or hesitancy such as the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines Survey, which measures vaccine hesitancy among parents; 19 the Vaccination Confidence Scale, which measures confidence in adolescent vaccination; 20 the 5-C scale (confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility), which identifies psychological barriers of vaccination behaviour; 21 and the SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale, which has been deployed across multiple countries.

span.label: THE THREE Cs HAVE BECOME FIVE AND ONE OF THE ORIGINALS IS GONE. macdonald2015's model was CONFIDENCE, COMPLACENCY, CONVENIENCE. The 5-C scale named here is `confidence, complacency, CONSTRAINTS, CALCULATION, and COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY`. Convenience is not in it, and nothing in this paper marks the substitution
span.quote: The VCI survey is one of a diverse set of metrics and indices used to measure confidence or hesitancy such as the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines Survey, which measures vaccine hesitancy among parents; 19 the Vaccination Confidence Scale, which measures confidence in adolescent vaccination; 20 the 5-C scale (confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility), which identifies psychological barriers of vaccination behaviour; 21 and the SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale, which has been deployed across multiple countries.

span.label: `conversely` - the word doing the work in `factors modulating vaccine confidence AND, CONVERSELY, HESITANCY`. It treats the two as opposite ends of one axis, which is precisely what macdonald2015 argued they are not: confidence is one of three categories of hesitancy determinant, not its inverse
span.quote: Factors modulating vaccine confidence and, conversely, hesitancy include (but are not limited to) trust in health-care systems, providers, governance, information, and perceptions of vaccine importance, safety, and efficacy.
